title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — variable window + HashMap.
shortTitle: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — Variable Window + HashMap

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge and uses a hash map from character to its last seen index to jump the left edge past any earlier occurrence of a repeated character, keeping the window free of duplicates. It runs in O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet)) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a stream of session tokens and wants the longest run with no repeated character, as a quick uniqueness signal. Rajesh keeps a window of recent characters and a note of where he last saw each one. When a repeat appears inside the window, he slides the left edge forward to just after the previous copy so the window is clean again.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow the window on the right, and when a character repeats inside it, jump the left edge to just past that character's previous position using a last-seen map.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge and uses a hash map from character to its last seen index to jump the left edge past any earlier occurrence of a repeated character, keeping the window free of duplicates. It runs in O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a stream of session tokens and wants the longest run with no repeated character, as a quick uniqueness signal. Rajesh keeps a window of recent characters and a note of where he last saw each one. When a repeat appears inside the window, he slides the left edge forward to just after the previous copy so the window is clean again.

**One line to remember:** Grow the window on the right, and when a character repeats inside it, jump the left edge to just past that character's previous position using a last-seen map.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain `left = 0`, a `best = 0`, and a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` holding the last index where each character was seen. For each `right`, look at `c = s.charAt(right)`. If `c` is in the map and its stored index is at least `left`, it means `c` appears inside the current window, so move `left` to `map.get(c) + 1` to drop that earlier copy. Then record `map.put(c, right)` and update `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)`.

A code snippet on a token string: `int longestUnique(String s) { Map<Character,Integer> last = new HashMap<>(); int l=0, best=0; for (int r=0; r<s.length(); r++) { char c=s.charAt(r); if (last.containsKey(c) && last.get(c) >= l) l = last.get(c) + 1; last.put(c, r); best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); } return best; }`. The condition `last.get(c) >= l` is essential: a stored index before `left` refers to a copy already outside the window and must be ignored.

The reason the left pointer never moves backward is that we always set it to one past the previous occurrence only when that occurrence is inside the window. Combined with each `right` advancing once, this gives linear time. The map lookups and updates are constant on average.

A senior nuance is that forgetting the `>= left` check causes a bug where a stale earlier index incorrectly pulls the left pointer backward, shrinking or corrupting the window. For a fixed small alphabet like lowercase letters you can replace the map with an int array of size 26 or 128 for ASCII, which is faster and uses fixed space. The map version is the general answer for arbitrary characters.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India security service inspects session token strings and wants the longest run of distinct characters as a cheap entropy heuristic to flag weak tokens. This is exactly how longest-substring-without-repeating works — a clean window of unique characters.

Problem 2 — Tokens can be long and arbitrary characters, so a general hash map keyed by character is used rather than a fixed small array.

The code shows a `TokenEntropyAnalyzer` with `longestDistinctRun`, a demo on a token string, and the longest distinct length.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: token "abcabcbb".

Step 1: Right at index 0 'a', not seen, map a→0, window "a" width 1, best 1. Right 1 'b', not seen, map b→1, window "ab" width 2, best 2. Right 2 'c', map c→2, window "abc" width 3, best 3.

Step 2: Right 3 'a', 'a' last seen at index 0 which is at least left 0, so left jumps to 1. Map a→3, window is "bca" width 3, best stays 3.

Step 3: Right 4 'b', 'b' last seen at index 1 which is at least left 1, so left jumps to 2. Map b→4, window "cab" width 3. Right 5 'c', last seen 2 at least left 2, left jumps to 3, map c→5, window "abc" width 3.

Step 4: Right 6 'b', last seen 4 at least left 3, so left jumps to 5. Map b→6, window "cb" width 2. Right 7 'b', last seen 6 at least left 5, left jumps to 7, map b→7, window "b" width 1.

Step 5: The maximum width recorded was 3, from "abc" at the start. The method returns 3.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Longest distinct run in 'abcabcbb': 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The longest substring without repeating characters is a variable-size sliding window problem backed by a map that remembers where each character was last seen. I advance the right edge one character at a time, and whenever the current character has a previous occurrence that lies inside the current window, I jump the left edge to one position past that previous occurrence so the window becomes duplicate-free again. After each step I update the best length from the current window width.

The detail that makes or breaks this solution is checking that the stored previous index is at least the current left pointer before I jump. A character might have been seen earlier but already fallen outside the window, and if I blindly moved the left pointer to that stale index I would pull it backward and corrupt the window. The at-least-left guard ensures the left pointer only ever moves forward, which both keeps correctness and guarantees linear time because each index is visited once on the right and the left pointer never resets.

For arbitrary characters I use a hash map keyed by character, but when the alphabet is small and fixed, such as lowercase letters or ASCII, I can replace the map with a small integer array for speed and fixed memory. The algorithm is otherwise identical.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the security service to measure the longest run of distinct characters in session token strings as a cheap entropy heuristic that flagged suspiciously weak tokens. Because tokens used arbitrary characters, the general hash-map version fit best. Explaining the window expansion, the last-seen map, and especially the at-least-left guard that keeps the pointer from moving backward shows the interviewer I understand the correctness subtlety that trips up most candidates.
